If he lets it go out, his vital breaths might depart from him.

O Agni, go to the one who hates us and to the wealth of those who hate us; taking them, depart to other distant realms. O Agni, being led forward in the rite for the ancestors and being extinguished, bestow here upon us progeny and long life.
When it is said: "O Agni, you who have been brought forward for those who are heedless become extinguished;
O Agni, that [extinguishment] of yours is well-ordered, and we kindle you again," one should bring forward the fire and inflame it.
With the two verses beginning "Thou art the belly of Indra" (PS 20.10.9; ŚS 7.111.1), he should place two fuel-sticks upon the fire.
Now, if the sacrificial post should sprout while the ritual is not yet completed, one should offer an oblation there with [the verse]: "The sacrificial post,
sprouting with a hundred branches, the sacrifice itself, encompassing and intending to delude the world of the sacrificer—
protected by the Vedas, surrounded by the Brahman, and stilled by the Atharvans— may it go to the world of the doers of good."
The sacrificial post has indeed ascended for the slaying of enemies; may neither my sacrifice nor the sacrificer suffer harm.
Place this sacrifice and the sacrificer in that world where the Seven Seers, the doers of good deeds, dwell. (KauśS 125.2)

Whatever affliction has befallen the trees, or whatever terrible thing has come upon our houses—that we drive out with this oblation of clarified butter. May it be well with our bipeds; may it be well with our quadrupeds.
"Whatever affliction has come upon the trees, or whatever marvel has come to our sacrifice—may all that be offered as a portion, O Agni; may we cross over to auspicious strengths.
Svāhā to Tvaṣṭṛ! Having thus offered the oblation.
With the mantra, "May Tvaṣṭṛ [make] my word divine" (*tvaṣṭā me daivyaṃ vacaḥ*), one should sacrifice a multi-colored animal dedicated to Tvaṣṭṛ.
Furthermore, if the sacrificial post should fall while the ritual is not yet completed, one should offer an oblation there.

Whether it was released by Indra or by the Maruts, that sacrificial post which has fallen for the destruction of our enemies—we drive it out with an oblation of clarified butter. May there be well-being for our bipeds, may there be well-being for our quadrupeds.
Having offered with "Svāhā to Tvaṣṭṛ," [one recites] "May Tvaṣṭṛ [grant] me divine speech" [as noted above].
"Thus, one should sacrifice a Tvaṣṭṛ-animal possessing all forms.
Now, if a crow should alight upon the sacrificial post while the ritual is not yet completed, one should offer an oblation there with [the verse]:
"Flow forth, O Soma, bringing gold, bringing horses, and bringing heroes."
"Bring us strength consisting of cattle, svāhā!"— having poured [the remainder] into the middle with these words, he should conclude the rite with the portions of the *saṃsrāva* (overflowing drops).

To Bhūḥ, svāhā!

these indeed are the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) of the gods.
These very [priests] perform for him that which is offered and sacrificed.

If, while the *prayāja* offerings have not yet been made, a glowing coal should fall before [the altar], there would be misfortune for the *adhvaryu*, the sacrificer, and the cattle; if it falls toward the south, there would be misfortune for the *brahman* and the sacrificer.
If there should be misfortune for the *pratyag-dhotṛ* and the wife,

With this verse, "He who has a thousand horns" (RV 10.90.1), [he should perform the rite]. // 6 //

He should offer an eight-potherd cake (*puroḍāśa*) to Agni Vīti;

When the oblations have been completed, one should pour [the remnants] into the center with the verse, "O Agni, come for the feast, being praised for the giving of the oblation; sit down as the Hotṛ upon the sacrificial grass" (SV 1.1), and conclude the rite with the portions of the *saṃsrāva*.
Now, if one's fires should become mixed with a village fire, what is the expiation for that?
He should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vivici. The regular fore-offerings are performed as before.
In the case of completed oblations:
"Agni, the domestic priest, the separator, the bestower of jewels—may he prolong our lives. (RV 1.1.1)
Having thus poured [the oblation] into the middle, he should conclude the rite with the portions of the remnants.
Now, if one's fires should become mixed with the fire of a corpse, what is the expiation for that?
He should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Śuci.
The *pūrvahoma*s are obligatory;
[they are performed] at the *saṃsthita-homa*s:
"Agni is the most pure in his vows, pure as a sage, pure as a seer."
The pure one, being offered oblations, shines forth.
"O Agni, your pure, bright, and radiant flames rise up;
your lights and rays—*svāhā*! Having poured [the oblation] into the center with these words, he should conclude the rite with the portions of the remnants.

(AVPr 2.7:87/16–17) Now, if one's fires should be mixed with a forest fire, what is the expiation for that? This [fire] indeed seizes the food of the sacrificer and turns back; he then approaches the village from the wilderness.
He should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni, the eater of food, the lord of food.

The obligatory offerings (*nityā homāḥ*) are performed before the concluding offerings (*saṃsthitahoma*). [In these concluding offerings: "May I not be behind the food on the road" (*apaścādaghvānnasya bhūyāsam*).
Having thus poured [the remnants] into the middle, he should conclude the rite with the portions of the *saṃsrāva*.
Now, if one's fires should become commingled with a divine fire, what is the expiation (*prāyaścitti*) in that case?
He should offer a cake on eight potsherds (*aṣṭākapāla-puroḍāśa*) to Agni Jyotiṣmat.
The obligatory offerings (*nitya-homa*) are performed before [the main rite];
likewise for the offerings at the conclusion (*saṃsthita-homa*).
[The formulas are: "It lightens, it flashes."
"Agni is the tongue of lightning;
by lightning they shine, they flash, and they gleam.
Having poured [the oblation] into the middle with these words, he should conclude the rite with the portions of the remnants.
Now, if one's fires should be extinguished, what is the expiation for that?
He should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Apsumat.
The regular *purastāddhoma* oblations are performed first.
When the oblations have been completed, having poured [the remnants] into the center with the verse,
"Agni with his bodies [is within the waters]" (AVŚ 5.7.8; ŚS 4.15.10),
he should conclude the rite with the portions of the residues.
Now, if one should rekindle a fire that has gone out, what is the expiation for that? He should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Agnimat;
the regular fore-offerings are performed as usual.
At the conclusion of the oblations:
"May you two be auspicious for us today" (KauśS 108.2);
"Fire is united with fire, the wise one, the lord of the house, the youth, the bearer of oblations, whose mouth is the sacrificial ladle" (KauśS 108.2).
"For you, O Agni, are kindled by fire; as a sage by a sage, being what you are, as a friend by a friend. (KauśS 108.2)
"Grant us great heroic strength" (RV 5.13.5c; SS 20.108.3c)—having thus poured [the butter] into the middle, he should then conclude the rite with the portions of the *saṃsrāva* (residue). // 7 //
Now, if one who has established the sacred fires should die while away on a journey during the performance of a ritual, how should one act in that case?
How should they offer his *agnihotra*?
They say: with the milk of a cow whose calf is different [from the one used for the sacrifice], or of one that has not yet calved, or of one milked by a *śūdra*.
"The milk of a cow that has another's calf, or of one milked by a Śūdra, is not complete; likewise, the Agnihotra of one who is dead is not complete.
They should tend the fire only until the collection of the bones.
Having collected them and touched them with the fires, they should conclude the rite with the Pitṛmedha."

Now, if one should die when the fires have been both formally consigned and not yet formally consigned, what should he do in that case? He should offer a sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) on one potsherd, seven potsherds, or nine potsherds to Agni Tantumat, Pathikṛt, and Vratapati.
The regular *purastāddhoma* offerings take place beforehand.
At the conclusion of the oblations:
"O Agni, you are far-extending... (as cited above);
"...by which path Vaivasvata... (as cited above).
"O Agni, you are the guardian of vows" (as cited above)— having poured [the butter] into the middle [of the fire], he should then conclude the rite with the portions of the remnants.

Now, if the two fire-drills should be lost, one should produce fire by rubbing another pair of fire-drills, and having offered with these very same [verses], they should then complete the rite with that [fire].
Now, if the animal that has been dedicated should fall away, what is the expiation for that?
One should offer oblations with *spṛti* verses to Vāyu Niyutvat; having prepared a gruel of barley, one should sacrifice another animal of the same form and the same color.
Having sprinkled it with clarified butter and performed the *paryagni* rite, one should dedicate it.
These indeed are the "spellers" (*devaspṛtayaḥ*) of the gods:
"O Agni, I spell your speech, svāhā!
From Vāta I spell your breath, svāhā!"
From the sun I preserve your sight, svāhā! From the moon I preserve your mind, svāhā! From the quarters I preserve your light, svāhā!
From the waters I secure your essence, svāhā!
From the bones I secure your marrow, svāhā!
From the fats I secure your sinews, svāhā!
From the plants I protect your body hair, svāhā!
From the earth I protect your physical frame, svāhā! From the intermediate space I protect your ether, svāhā!
From the human for you I secure the divine space, svāhā!
From Indra for you I secure strength, svāhā!
From King Soma for you I secure renown and glory, svāhā!
Having offered thus, he then points it out again with the words, "To Vāyu thee" (*vāyave tvā*).
Now, if the animal that has been dedicated should die, what is the expiation (*prāyaścitti*) in that case?
Having offered with the *spṛti* verses, he then assigns it [to the deity] with the formula:
"For the Ṛta, thee!
Now, if the animal that has been brought forward should break apart, what is the expiation (*prāyaścitti*) in that case?
Having offered with the *spṛti* verses, he then assigns this [offering] to them with the words,
"To the Rākṣasas, thee!
Some say that there is no such thing as an assignment (*anudeśana*).
Or, if this [animal] has fallen down, then if they should find it, he should sacrifice with it.

Now, regarding these two that have died of old age: one should cut off their well-known portions, or else, having given the call for another animal, the Brahmins should serve [the guests] or offer water with the *spṛti* verses.

Or if there should be another [fire], they should lead it to the *śāmitra* fire... having offered with the *iṣṭi*-offerings, they should indeed lead it to the *śāmitra* fire. From this point onward, the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*) is well-established.
Now, if one should officiate for one who is afflicted by illness, what is the expiation (*prāyaścitti*) in that case?
Having offered with the *spṛti* verses alone, one indeed becomes free from sin.
Now, if there should be many who are afflicted by illness, what is the expiation in that case? Having offered with the *spṛti* verses alone, one indeed becomes free from sin.

Now, if the sacrificer should die while the *agnihotra* has been placed on the fire, what should he do in that case? He should place it right there so that it may burn completely. Then, he should offer an oblation of clarified butter (*ājya*) into the *āhavanīya* fire.

With this verse, "The sacrifice goes forth, spread out and being prepared" (PS 18.77.3; ŚS 18.4.13), [one should proceed]. Now, if the sacrificer should die on the day of the fast (aupavasathya), how should one act in that case?
In that very place he should apply this [mantra] so that it may be completely consumed;
then he should offer an oblation of clarified butter into the Āhavanīya fire with [the verse]:
"The sacrifice goes forth, spread out and being prepared... (as cited above).
With this verse [one should act].

Now, if the sacrificer should die when the oblations are already prepared, how should one proceed in that case? In that situation, one should place them on the fire in such a way that they are completely consumed by the flames.
Then he should offer an oblation of clarified butter into the Āhavanīya fire with this verse: "The living ones have driven him away from his homes" (RV 10.87.21).
Now, if one who has been consecrated (*dīkṣita*) should die, how should they cremate him?
"With those very same fires," they say.
"For these are my *havyavāhana* (carriers of oblations to the gods); let them now become my *kavyavāhana* (carriers of oblations to the ancestors)."
"Now then, how is it?
"Having filled three fire-pans with balls of dung, they should place them [on the fire];
they should shake them."
They should complete [the rite] with those fires that are produced as very hot;
or rather, they become external, and thus these do not [belong] to them.

The Brāhmaṇa for that [rite] is the same as that which was explained regarding the blessings (*āśis*) in the Pitṛmedha at the *adaḥpurasavana*. If someone should speak ill of him while he is standing in front, one should say to him:
"I place you within the gaping mouth of the Vasu gods."
"Recite the Gāyatrī; fall down with your head downward! (AVPr 2.9:93/18–20).
If someone should revile him while he is standing on the south side, he should say to that person:
"I place you within the gaping mouth of the Rudras, the gods."
"Fall down head-first into the *parṣā* of the *triṣṭubh*!
If he should speak ill of him while he is standing behind, he should say to him:
"I place you within the gaping mouth of the Āditya gods."
"Fall down headfirst into the assembly of the Jāgata!"—
if one should revile him while he is standing to the north, he should say to him:
"I place you within the gaping mouth of all the gods."
"Fall down with your head downward into the assembly of the *anuṣṭubh*!"—
if someone should revile him while he is standing in the intermediate regions, one should say to him:
"One should pay homage to him."
If he should return the salutation, one should engage him with well-being. If he should not return the salutation, one should perform sorcery against him.
One should circumambulate [the fire] to the left, keeping it to the right, without tying a knot, using the fires.
"Thou art the year, thou art the full year, thou art the complete year"—with these words [he should touch him].
If he should wish to strike him down, [he should recite]:
"Of whom all... [PS 19.55.1].
With this hymn, one should place the *bādhakī* fuel-sticks upon the fire.
The following—(the third day: cf. 19.55.2e, 3e, 4d;
*ucchiṣṭaḥ*: 19.55.1d)—suggests that it has...
On the third day, he does not live beyond that.
Now, whatever remains as an offering-residue when the oblation has been half-offered by the Hotṛ, having sipped water together with that [residue], [he recites]:
"May Agni protect me with the Vasus from the east" [PS 7.16.1].
Having recited this, one should act according to the truth; one should act according to the truth. // 9 //
Thus ends the second chapter on expiations for sacrifices.
[Ed. *purastād*] Now, therefore, we shall explain the forms of Soma.
Prajāpati was in the mind.
The *sārasvata* [offering] is [recited] when speech is released;
the ritual procedure [is performed] during the initiation (*dīkṣā*).
In the *brahma-vrata*, while the *savitṛ* [rite] is being joined, [the verse] "blind, mindless, divine, fair-winged" (*andho 'cheto divyaḥ suparṇaḥ*) is recited as a circumambulation.
Aditi at the introductory offering;
established among cattle when scattered;
the sacrifice being offered.
The auspicious one being sifted;
the meters being measured;
fortune being staked.
Asura is [the deity] when [the soma] has been purchased;
Varuṇa when it has been bound with a cord;
Pūṣan when it is on the path leading to the purchase of the soma.
Śipiviṣṭa when being seated;
Bṛhaspati when rising;
Vāyu when being carried forward.
The presiding deity when being carried forward is Agni-Soma; the sacrificial animal is Rudra, the guest.
Varuṇa at the constant hospitality;
Varuṇa as the sovereign ruler;
[Varuṇa] being seated upon the throne-seat.
The *aindrāgna* [verse] when the fire is being churned;
the *aindrāgna* when the fire is being led forward;
the *sāman* at the *tānūnaptra* rite.
Austerity is performed during the intermediate consecration;
the earth during the Upasad; and the intermediate space during the Upasad.
The sky is the *upasat*;
the measure of the sacrifice is the counterpart when the altar is being prepared;
the cattle are on the *uttaravedi*.
Heaven is in the two Havirdhāna sheds; the intermediate space is in the Āgnīdhrīya shed;
the earth is in the Sadas. // 1 //
The vital breaths are in the *uparava* pits;
the rivals are in the *dhiṣṇya* hearths;
the cattle are in the sacrificial grass (*barhis*).
When the sacrificial altar is being strewn;
when [the oblation] is cast into the waters;
and when Prajāpati is being carried away.
Agni [is invoked] at the Āgnīdhrīya fire;
Viṣṇu [is invoked] during the ritual action involving the offering ladle;
the hand is released.
The sacrificial post belongs to Viṣṇu;
the plants are in the girdle;
the sacrificial essence is in the Āprī verses.
The oblation when it has been carried around the fire;
the verse addressed to the Pitṛs while the sacrificial animal is being slaughtered;
and the couple of the sacrifice during the washing of the utensils.
The portion for the *rakṣas* is [recited] when the omentum is being lifted up;
the continuity of the sacrifice is [recited] when the *vasatīvarī* waters are being brought forward;
he sets down the cow of Indra and Agni on the northern corner of the southern high altar (*uttaravedi*).
The cow of Mitra and Varuṇa:
he places it down on the northern corner of the northern high altar;
[the cow] of the Viśve Devas on the Āgnīdhrīya hearth.
The *chandasyas* [are recited] on the day of preparation (*upavasatha*);
the *havirupāvahṛtaḥ* [at the time] the oblation has been brought forward;
the *sārasvata* [is recited] during the morning litany (*prātaranuvāka*).
Atharvan [is the deity] when [the seed] has been sown;
Prajāpati when it is being divided;
the deities when it has been divided.
(Indra is the slayer of Vṛtra; Indra is the slayer of the adversary; Indra is the one who overcomes Vṛtra, being drawn up.
(The *āyus* formula belongs to the *upāṃśu* and *antaryāma* cups. Yama has been declared [as the deity]. 2.

In the *nibhūya* and *purādhāvanīya* [verses], [the Soma] is well-purified in the *pūtabhṛt* vessel; it possesses the splendor of pure juice, the splendor of the stirred drink (*mantha*), the splendor of parched grain (*saktu*), and the splendor of milk; [it is] the *kakubh* meters in the vessels.
Vāyu is [the deity] in the *bahiṣpavamāna*;
the *hotrās* are [the deities] in the *pravara*.
The Vasus [are the deities] in the *prayāja* offerings;
the animal sacrifice has the same deity as the Soma;
the *unnīyamāna* offering belongs to the Viśvedevas.
The offering for Indra and Agni has been drawn up;

the wind, the host of Maruts, has turned back toward us.
*nṛcakṣāḥ* when it is *pratikhyātaḥ*;
*bhakṣaḥ* when it is *bhakṣyamāṇaḥ*;
and *sakhā* when it is *bhakṣitaḥ*.
The Nārāśaṃsa cups belong to the ancestors.
The morning pressing belongs to Agni;
the midday pressing belongs to Indra.
The sacrifice is in the *dakṣiṇā*;
the *pṛṣṭha* stotras belong to Indra;
the third pressing belongs to the Viśvedevas.

The Aindrāvaruṇa becomes the Uktha of the Maitrāvaruṇa;
the Aindrābārhaspatya becomes the Uktha of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin.
The *uktha* of the Achāvāka belongs to Indra and Viṣṇu;
the *ṣoḍaśin* night belongs to Indra;
the *paryāya* belongs to Agni.
The *rāthaṃtara* is the junction;
the *saurya* and the *āśvina*;
the day and the sacrifice.
The Ādityas are in the after-offerings;
that which is performed between them is the ocean;
Varuṇa is in the purificatory bath.
"O ocean, in the dregs! (AVPr 3.3:96/15).
That which is on this side of the ford is the *prāyaṇīya*;
that which is beyond it is the *udayanīya*. (AVPr 3.3:96/16)
The *vaiṣṇava* [verse] is used for the barren cow (*vaśā*);
"In heaven, the light" (*svar divi*) [is used] for the *kāsu*; and the *brahma samiṣṭyā* [verse is used] for the *samiṣṭiyajus*. // 3 //
If the Soma should be spoiled at the end of any [offering], one should perform an *iṣṭi* sacrifice for that respective deity, or offer oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*).
Then one should recite:
"The sacrifice is you, O Viṣṇu," and so forth.
"May the sacrifice, Viṣṇu, and the two—sacrifice and Viṣṇu—not abandon you, but make myself known among the gods as complete.
"O Lord of the Forest, may I be at the end," [he says]. Regarding the *anuṣṭubh* meter, he recites that which was addressed to it: "With this I join together.
Having joined it, [he recites] "What of mine has spilled" [as mentioned above] when there has been a spilling.
That which is expressed by "if there is a lapse of memory" (PS 20.8.9;
ŚS 7.106.1) and "in the reversal of the ritual action," that is [the mantra] "oṃ bhūr janad" from the Ṛgveda (cf. GB 1.3.3e).
Thus one should offer into the Gārhapatya fire.

If [the error occurred] regarding the Yajus, one should offer into the Dakṣiṇāgni fire with "oṃ bhuvo janat. If [the error occurred] regarding the Sāman, one should offer into the Āhavanīya fire with "oṃ svar janat."
If [the rite] is according to the Atharvaveda, one should offer into the Āhavanīya fire itself with the formula: "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svar janad oṃ. Then follow the deities;
the office of the Hotṛ belongs to Agni.
The office of the Adhvaryu belongs to Vāyu;
the office of the Udgātṛ belongs to Sūrya;
the office of the Brahman belongs to Candra.
Agni was indeed his Hotṛ;
Vāyu was the Adhvaryu;
Sūrya was the Udgātṛ.
The moon is Brahman;
the earth is the abode of the *ṛc*s;
fire is the light of the intermediate space.
The abode of the *yajus* formulas is Vāyu; light and heaven are indeed the abode of the *sāman* chants.
"The sun is the light; water is the abode of the Atharvans; the moon is the light"—thus it is said. 4.

Now, as for what we said regarding "the Soma in the event of a transgression": if they should first seize the King Soma from the sacrificer, or if he should suffer a mental derangement—so says Āśmarathya.
"No," say Kāṇva and Gopāyana.
"The teachers say: 'At the very moment that a ritual act is prescribed for the Adhvaryu, at that same moment calamities are prescribed with respect to all sacrifices.
Now, how then can there be ritual acts belonging to the sacrificer in this case?"
The Adhvaryu priest, being the one who partakes of the ritual offerings, shall perform the duties of this sacrificer.

Here, having placed two *camasa* cups either on the sacrificer’s seat or at the *mārjālīya* hearth, they should set out the portions for his consumption there from the time of the *bhakṣa* until the offering of the *samiṣṭayajus*.
If the sacrificer should arrive prior to the offering of the *samiṣṭayajus*, he should recite all the *bhakṣa*-mantras together and then consume the remainder.
Having completed the avabhṛtha bath, they should proceed together.
Now, if one should not come within the range of hearing while still alive, for how long a time should they offer the *agnihotra* for him?
If his allotted lifespan has been fully calculated, they should offer that *agnihotra* for him for that much time, and then proceed with his *prāyaṇīya* rite.
The application of the vessels has also been explained, just as in the case of the body not being visible.
If he should return while still alive, or if he has returned after having gone abroad, one should perform for him the rites as required.

If he has risen on his own accord, one should establish the fires for him again and recite the *adbhuta* formulas. Having offered the oblations and performed the ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*), this person who has returned may then perform the rites.
If, however, it should not be rekindled, his *agnihotra* remains established exactly as it was.
For there is a scriptural revelation (*śruti*) stating: "This *sattra*, namely the *agnihotra*, lasts until old age. 6.
(AVPr 3.7:98/14–16) Now, if one who has established the sacred fires should die while living abroad, how should one understand the disposal of the vessels in that case?
Thus said Āśmarathya:

(AVPr 3.7:98/17–18) If they have set aside other vessels as sacrificial implements, having carried forward the fire, kindled it, and then distributed it—or having kindled a fire produced by friction—they should distribute it.

Having thus concluded with these [verses] beginning with "aṅga," one should cover [the site] with the ritual formula "pātraviniyoga. Whatever vessels may have been lost, including the *vāraṇī* [ladle], one should cast them into the water with the verse "eṣā te agne."
"O Agni, by that [path] do thou ascend for me; by that do thou enter for me"—with these words, one should give objects made of stone or iron to the Brāhmaṇas.
For ten nights, they should remain observant of their vows.

When the ritual has commenced, whether in its initial stage or its internal stage, if the householder (*gṛhapati*) falls ill, one may—having taken his life-force (*āyus*)—follow [the rite]; having consecrated (*upadīkṣya*) his son or brother as he desires, they may complete the sacrifice, or they may not complete it.

No, says Āśmarathya;
for there is no secondary initiation (*upadīkṣā*) for the householder.
Having looked at the householder, if he should think,
"May this man live for a day and a night," then during one-day rites (whether involving one or two overnight stays), he should cause him to enter all the *savana*s.
But whichever *savana* one should cause [the rites] to enter, the others come under its control;

even if the *savanas* have different ritual procedures (*tantra*), if one desires to perform the *iṣṭis* together in a combined performance (*samāsa*) when there is a difficult situation, one should cause them to enter that [primary] *savana*.

Whatever *iṣṭis* may be of a single ritual procedure (*ekatantra*) and uninterrupted, one may at will cause them to enter that single *tantra* and proceed with the oblations (*havis*) in their proper sequence.
Before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, one should offer five oblations of clarified butter into the mouth [of the fire]:

Now, therefore, we shall explain the procedure for those engaged in a sacrificial session (*sattra*). When the ritual has commenced, the fuel and the sacrificial grass have been bound together, and one should look at the moon from behind—
[that which belongs to them...]
On the Vāsī day, there is a cake for Agni; he performs that as the Pāthikṛt sacrifice, omitting the rest according to the archetype.

Now, if one’s full-moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsya*) should be impaired, he may at his will perform the archetypal rites (*prākṛtīḥ*) therein.
Then, whichever sacrifice exists— whether it be the *dyāvākṛto* or the *vāyo*— he offers it.
Having placed the oblations—a cake on eight potsherds for Agni and a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra—one should offer the expiatory oblations with [the verse]:
"That greatness of his which has risen from the great, the majesty of this earthly world—may no other misfortune whatsoever reach us.
(AVPr 3.10:101/4–6) [Note: The edition reads *uchunā*, cf. PS 19.16.5d.]

For example:

"Having offered the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ oblation with the formula: 'The intermediate space [he offered] with his limbs, the sacrifice with his members, the earth with his bodies; O Lord of Speech, with unimpaired speech, with an unimpaired ladle, he sent the Hotṛ who increases the gods to heaven—Svāhā! Prajāpati would then release this entire world.
For such indeed is the Vedic revelation. 10.

If they should cause the *sānnāyya* to overflow, or if the calves [should do so], [the offering belongs to] Vāyu.
One should perform the *sāṃnāyya* sacrifice with barley-gruel (*yavāgū*).
Even if there is only one cow that has calved, one should have her milked.
Having completed the rite with the cows that have already calved, and having set aside the calves of those that have not yet calved, one should perform the *sāṃnāyya* sacrifice on the following day.
If they should steal the evening milking, one should divide the morning milking into two parts; having placed one part in the place of the evening milking, one should sacrifice with both.
If they should steal the morning milking, one should divide the evening milking into two parts; having placed one part in the place of the morning milking, one should sacrifice with both.

If both should become spoiled, one should prepare a five-platter rice-offering for Indra; having performed the rite with the offering for Agni, one should subsequently perform the rite with the offering for Indra, and having fasted on the following day...

If all the sacrificial oblations (*havīṃṣi*) should be stolen or become defiled, one should sacrifice to the deities with clarified butter (*ājya*).
Then, one should perform another faultless *iṣṭi* sacrifice;
they should consume the defiled water,
and the defiled sacrificial oblation (*havis*) which is unfit to be eaten by Brahmins.

If the clarified butter should spill while it has already been prepared, one should measure out the directions with three spans, saying: "To Bhūpati, svāhā! The formula *tad yajamāno devāñ janam agan* ("thereby the sacrificer has gone to the gods and the people") is to be appended.
One should enclose [the spilt butter] with four formulas beginning with *yajñasya tvā pramaye*.
[The full formulas are: *yajñasya tvā pramayā*, *unmayā*, *abhimayā*, and *pratimayā paridadema svāhā*.
If unclarified ghee (*ājya*) should spill, one should offer wealth and breath (*prāṇa*).

Likewise, if clarified ghee (*ghṛta*) that has been purified or is being purified should spill, one should offer wealth; if clarified ghee that has been purified or is being purified should spill when there is a change of deity, one should offer breath.

One should offer the universal expiation with the verses "tvaṃ no agne" and "sa tvaṃ na."

(AYVPr 4.1:105/6–8) "O Agni, you who are wise, may you remove from us the wrath of the god Varuṇa; being the best of sacrificers, the most excellent bearer of oblations, and brightly shining, release from us all those who hate us. (RV 4.1.4)
"O Agni, be our protector, most helpful and nearest to us at the dawning of this very Uṣas;
being gracious, appease Varuṇa for us; grant us mercy, and be easy for us to invoke—Svāhā! (RV 4.1.5). Thus [it is said].

If, during the offering to the deity, there should be an exchange of the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses, or if there should be an obstruction regarding the *ṛc* in cases where no expiation has been prescribed, one should offer an oblation in the *gārhapatya* fire with the mantra: "bhūr janad."

If the Brahman priest is unaware [of the deity], he should offer into the Āhavanīya fire itself at the conclusion of the *ājyabhāga* offerings, saying: "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svar janad oṃ. Intending to invoke the deity for whom the oblation has been set aside, he should sacrifice with that [deity] after having poured out these portions of clarified butter (*ājya*).

If there is a crack in the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), he should sacrifice from that part which is not cracked.

if a potsherd is lost, one should give a one-year-old calf.
"May Dhātṛ, the father of the father, establish [the sacrifice]; the Gharma is unharmed, possessing all life, from which he was born; from that [place] may he protect us, svāhā!
[Thus one should offer].

One should prepare a cake on one potsherd for Agni, one on two potsherds for the Aśvins, one on three potsherds for Viṣṇu, and one on four potsherds for Soma.

"May we have good offspring; for you have granted me a hundredfold [blessing]. O gods, bestow great protection upon us here!
Having said this, [he recites] "The thousand-horned one... (PS 18.16.2).

"Make us hearers of the Soma, O Brahmaṇaspati, as Kakṣīvat was for Auśija" (RV 1.18.1);
"So do thou for us, O Agni" (see above);
"The bull of the people, omniform, invincible, Bṛhaspati the excellent" (RV 3.62.6).

One should offer oblations with these [verses]: "Loosen the uppermost bond for us, untie the middle bond, and cast away the lower ones" (cf. RV 1.25.21); and "Loosen the uppermost, O Varuṇa" (PS 18.82.6; ŚS 7.83.3 / 18.4.69). // 1 //

Having taken hold of her right hand with the words, "I am he; you are she," he should summon her. If an oblation should spill outside the enclosing sticks, they should say to the Āgnīdhra, "We shall enclose it; offer it."

To him he should give a full vessel. "Do not harm us, O god, sent forth; be strengthened by the splendor of the clarified butter (*ājya*). Do not injure anything of ours.
For the sake of the peace of acquisition and preservation (*yogakṣema*), sit upon this sacrificial grass (*barhis*).
If the ritual action has been heated, [it is] a subordinate element (*guṇa*).

"The sacrifice itself becomes the expiation for the sacrifice.

If it should spill from the time of milking until the time of the oblation—

Having consecrated [the water] with this mantra—
(“Lift us up from the highest...
and (“O Varuṇa, lift us up from the highest...”)— [one should proceed].
Thus, one should offer oblations of clarified butter with the Vāruṇī verse:
"samudraṃ tvā... (which is the Paippalāda version of the mantra).
The Śāṅkhāyana Śrautasūtra says: "samudraṃ vaḥ. (AVPr 4.3:115–116). [Regarding the *chāvalī* offering: O God, if one's evening oblation should be spilled, he shall not eat in the morning.

Having placed a fuel-stick with the verse, "Mitra impels men" (RV 3.59.1), and having milked another [cow], he should sacrifice again.
(Mitra, speaking, impels men; Mitra has supported the earth and the sky;
Mitra gazes upon the people with unblinking eyes; offer an oblation rich in ghee to Mitra—*svāhā*!

If insects have fallen into it, one should throw it into an anthill with the verse *hiraṇyagarbhaḥ* (PS 4.1.1; ŚS 4.2.7), milk another [cow], and offer again. // 3 //

The sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is a choice gift.

Having kindled the fires, the sacrificer and his wife—or both remaining without food and restraining their speech—should sit together throughout the entire day with the two fire-drills (*araṇī*) in their hands.

One should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Agni Vaiśvānara.
For if he should think ill of his offspring during the day, [he should recite]:
"In unison with Jātavedas, O Agni, partake of the oblation by day and through the earth; Svāhā! [cf. MS 1.8.6].

If he should not stop, [he should offer] another twelve-night period with the formula: "To Agni, the most easily kindled, be pleased; svāhā! Having missed the evening oblation of the night, he should set out the Agnihotra for the morning meal and sit by it until the sun sets.
Having completed the ritual, one should offer an oblation with the formula: "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svar janad doṣā vastoḥ svāhā.

Then, for the daily morning worship performed day after day and night after night, one should offer an oblation into the Gārhapatya fire with the *sruva* ladle, using the formula: "To Agni, accept this; svāhā!"

One should give food to that Brāhmaṇa whose food one would not otherwise eat; one should fetch a fuel-stick from below. One who is mindful of the Agnihotra should lay down the Darbha grass with their tips pointing toward the south. If both fires should go out while the sun sets or rises, or if they should be lost while in the fire-enclosing trench, or if they have not been properly rekindled, one should establish them again according to the original rite.
Thus ends the fourth chapter on expiations for sacrifices.
If the sun should set while the *agnihotra* fire has not been drawn out, a learned Brāhmaṇa should draw it out.
Whatever Brāhmaṇa is highly learned, he should draw it out.
With everything by which it is concealed, that Brāhmaṇa should draw it out, carrying gold in front of him.
"One should offer a sacrificial pap (*caru*) made of barley to Varuṇa;
[this is] first from this very [source]. "From this very [source] Agni Jātavedas was born, from these wombs."

Having placed the two kindling woods (*araṇī*) behind the mark of the *gārhapatya* fire with the verse, "May he, the god, knowing [the way], carry the oblation to the gods by means of the *gāyatrī*, the *triṣṭubh*, the *jagatī*, and the *anuṣṭubh*" (KauśS 133.6; TB 1.4.4.8), and having churned [the fire] with the mantra,
